newsitem.title: INDIA: India court drops corruption cases against leaders.
newsitem.headline: India court drops corruption cases against leaders.

text.p: An Indian court on Tuesday dropped money laundering cases against the chief of the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) party and a former government minister, news agencies said. The New Delhi High Court dismissed 1991 "hawala" money laundering cases against BJP president L.K. Advani, which had forced him to resign from parliament, and former Congress party minister Vidya Charan Shukla, they said.
More than 100 politicians and bureaucrats have been implicated in the $18-million scandal.

Seven ministers in former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao's government who were linked to the scandal resigned last year, only weeks before their Congress party suffered its worst ever defeat in general elections.
The United News of India (UNI) quoted High Court judge Mohammed Shamim as saying he had dismissed the cases against Advani and Shukla for lack of evidence.

The news agency quoted Shamim as saying that entries in a diary of alleged money-launderers used by India's federal police, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), to press charges against the two were not sufficient evidence.
BJP officials declared the verdict a victory for their party but declined to say if Advani would contest future elections.
"There could not be a better New Year's gift," Advani was quoted by UNI as saying. India's southern and western regions observed Tuesday as the beginning of the new Hindu year.
"The 15-month period since January 1996 has been a most trying and traumatic phase in my life," Advani added.
"It is by the grace of God and the unstinted support and good will extended by colleagues and supporters that I have come through this challenging period with satisfaction."
Advani resigned his parliamentary seat soon after he was indicted in January 1996, and vowed not to run for office until he was cleared of the charges.
The judge also dropped charges against three businessmen brothers who had been accused of being involved in money laundering.

The scandal had its roots in the chance arrest of two suspected Kashmiri guerrillas in March 1991 who put police on the track of J.K. Jain, later accused of being a dealer on the illegal foreign exchange market.
A diary found in the Jain home listed in code the names of 115 politicians and bureaucrats and gave details of payments that each were alleged to have received from him, federal investigators said.
They said the payments, between April 1988 and March 1991, totalled nearly 655 million rupees ($18.3 milion).
The Jain brothers, who run large engineering and fertiliser companies in northern Bihar state, were later accused of receiving political favours in return for the payments.
On Tuesday, Rao suffered a setback in another case when a judge overruled his objections and permitted a politician who has accused Rao of once buying votes to testify in a trial.

Shailendra Mahato, of the regional Jharkhand Mukti Morcha, has said Rao paid members of his party to help to defeat a no confidence motion against Rao's government in June 1993. Rao has denied the accusation.
On Tuesday, Judge Ajit Bharihoke permitted Mahato to turn state's witness in exchange for a pardon, officials said.
"All objections have been overruled," the judge told a crowded courtroom. "Mahato's application has been allowed. I have granted pardon."
$1 = 35.8 rupees
